Investment memo · Shell plc (SHEL-GB)

Shell: a well-run cash machine priced for a Hormuz windfall that is near its peak. Underwrite the cash, not the multiple.

Written 8-Nov-26 at a price of 4,033p (USD 53.98, the 23-Oct-26 price the model uses); market value USD 310bn. Next events: the Q4 update note in early January 2027, then Q4 results and the Capital Markets Update on 4-Feb-27. Bases, sources and abbreviations are in the end notes.

Summary: the key insights, implications and conclusions

What the analysis means for the decision

  1. Do not buy Shell at 4,033p. On my fair multiple of about 10x, the probability-weighted 18-month total return is about -7%, and the plausible range runs from -28% to +22%.
  2. If Shell is already held, hold it through the 4-Feb-27 Capital Markets Update. The three months to that update are the last period in which guidance, estimates and narrative all move the case's way.
  3. Plan to buy after the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz has de-rated the sector. At USD 42 a share (about 9x forward earnings), the three-year return at a 10x fair multiple is about +25%, with a cash yield of about 10% while waiting.
  4. Time the case with one weekly series: Hormuz energy-tanker transits. Transits run at about ten a day against 35 before the crisis; transits above 20 a day for a month would signal the reopening.
  5. Size any position for a 25-35% drawdown, which is the plausible fall in the most likely 18-month path.

The business. Shell is a high-quality harvest-and-return business. It has one genuine and widening moat: the world's largest LNG portfolio, backed by physical trading and by the freedom to send cargoes to whichever destination pays most. Its upstream business is mid-table, with the shortest proved reserve life among the European majors. Its management team has delivered every controllable target it has promised since 2023.

The windfall. In 2026 Shell is earning a geopolitical windfall. The Strait of Hormuz has been shut since March 2026, Brent is above USD 100, and Shell's FY2026 adjusted earnings are heading for about one and a half times what its normal engine earns.

The investment case. For the next 12-24 months, Shell's investment case turns on one variable, and that variable is not Shell: it is the state of the Strait of Hormuz. About 85% of the forecast change in earnings from FY2026 to FY2028 (a fall of about USD 13bn) comes from four price lines: Brent, the refining margin, European gas and the exceptional trading layer. All four price lines are readings of the same geopolitical state. Shell's own levers (ARC Resources, the Qatar and Pearl restoration, LNG Canada, costs and the chemicals exit) give back only about USD 3bn, and half of that USD 3bn also waits on the Strait reopening.

Six conclusions carry the memo.

1
Shell's cash and per-share lines are unusually predictable; its profit line is not.

In every plausible state of the Strait, FY2027 free cash flow after leases lands between USD 27bn and 38bn. Against that, the dividend costs about USD 9bn, the buyback is at least USD 12bn, and net debt excluding leases stays near zero (ex-lease gearing was 2.7% at Q3). The buyback floor holds down to USD 50 Brent and the dividend down to about USD 40. FY2027 EPS, by contrast, sits in a cone with three peaks, at about USD 4.2, 5.3 and 7.0 (probabilities of 30%, 45% and 25%), and that cone is three times the width normal for a company of Shell's size. Underwrite the cash; do not underwrite any single FY2027 EPS figure.

2
The skew in Shell's earnings is positive; the skew in its share price is negative.

The probability-weighted FY2027 EPS of about USD 5.4 sits above the base case (USD 5.30) and above consensus (USD 5.28 at 25-Oct-26, and rising since). The earnings skew is positive because the downside state is cushioned (by the LNG price lag, refining cracks lagging crude, the return of Qatar volumes, working-capital release and buybacks at a lower share price) and the upside state is large. The share-price skew is negative because each state hurts the multiple. The upside state brings windfall taxes, demand destruction and a sharper reopening later. The downside state de-rates the whole sector at the moment earnings fall. With Shell's 24-month-forward P/E at the 99th percentile of five years and near the 90th percentile of ten years, the multiple is at risk in both states.

3
The case has a three-month window in which everything moves Shell's way, then a long leg in which it does not.

The favourable window runs to the 4-Feb-27 Capital Markets Update and is built from dated, likely events: a strong Q4 print, estimate upgrades, a probable dividend-growth reset and a larger buyback. The adverse leg starts around mid-2027 in 70% of states, when FY2027 consensus is cut back and the sector de-rates. On estimates the two legs roughly cancel. On the multiple they do not cancel, because the multiple falls as the Strait's state resolves.

4
The forecasts ask almost nothing of Shell's management.

The model's mid-cycle adjusted earnings of USD 23-24bn by 2028 are USD 5-6bn above 2025. About USD 3.5bn of that increase is self-help already banked, plus ARC Resources and LNG Canada; the rest comes from the price deck. The only capability Shell has not demonstrated at scale, running a large North American shale business, is worth about USD 1bn of earnings in the window. Management risk is therefore low, and the risk to the case is almost entirely external.

5
The guideline fair multiple of 11.58x is the largest single risk to the return, larger than the earnings risk, and the two risks are correlated.

A multiple of 11.58x is the 90th percentile of Shell's own ten-year history, the band the dashboard labels "mania". About three-quarters of Shell's multiple is a sector phenomenon (the six-month R-squared against the European peer basket is 71%, and beta is 0.83), so Shell's multiple and Shell's earnings fall together when the Strait reopens. At 11.58x the model's 18-month total return is +4.3% and the three-year return +14.0%, almost all of it dividends, because a 6.7% re-rating merely offsets a 6.5% fall in forward EPS. My own fair multiple at the 18-month horizon is about 10x, which turns the 18-month return into roughly -10% and the three-year return into about nil.

6
Shell today is not the positively skewed setup Richard looks for; it is close to the mirror image of one.

The probability of guidance and estimate upgrades is unusually high for three months and unusually low thereafter. The fundamentals are at a peak that the market has correctly refused to capitalise beyond 2027, and the valuation leaves no cushion. The constructive reading is that the case is simple, binary and trackable from one weekly series (Hormuz transits), so it can be timed. The attractive entry comes after the reopening has de-rated the sector, when Shell's per-share engine (buybacks at a lower price, and USD 10-15bn of unused balance-sheet capacity by 2028) works for a buyer rather than against one.

Where my view differs from the market. I agree with the sell-side on the shape of earnings and on the quality of management. I differ on the length of the closure, on the multiple and on how much of the dividend reset is already priced.

Scorecard: the twelve topics

Shell scores well on delivery, internal change and momentum, and poorly on the forecasts, the risk and the return.

The five judgements that move the shares, with the arithmetic

The multiple and the Hormuz state each move the share price by more than 20%, and they move together. The one company-controlled driver, the 4-Feb-27 distribution reset, barely moves EPS and acts on the multiple instead.

The arithmetic uses the model's average diluted share count (about 5,490m for FY2027 and 5,205m for FY2028) and the second analysis set's post-tax sensitivities: about USD 330m per USD 1/bbl of Brent, USD 320m per USD 1/bbl of refining margin and USD 300m per USD 1/mmbtu of TTF gas.

Four of the five judgements are one judgement about the Strait. Judgements 1, 2, 4 and 5 are not independent: each is a reading of the Strait of Hormuz. If the Strait reopens fast, Brent falls, refining cracks normalise, trading fades, the sector de-rates and the normal deck is marked down, all together. If the Strait stays shut, the reverse happens until windfall taxes and demand destruction arrive. A Monte Carlo simulation that treated these lines as independent would therefore understate the width of the cone. Judgement 3 is the one company-controlled driver; its date is fixed, and its value runs through the multiple rather than through EPS.

1Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

Shell's operating environment is driven by supply scarcity, not demand, and the scarcity is at its peak. Almost every headwind is pro-cyclical to that tailwind: taxes, demand destruction and rates all grow the longer prices stay high, which is what makes the setup fragile.

Inference: the favourable part of the environment is its most cyclical part. The external picture is strongly favourable today, but the favourable part is at its peak, for three reasons. Refining margins are the most mean-reverting line (Redburn expected European margins to peak in Q3 2026). Crude is near the level that has historically triggered demand destruction and fiscal response. The structural supports act slowly.

Since 29-Oct-26 the evidence has leaned toward a longer closure of the Strait. The evidence for a longer closure is strong: Gulf states are planning for hostilities lasting up to ten years, three US carrier groups are in the region, Iran's drone capacity has been restored, a toll regime of USD 1-2m per transit is in place, and QatarEnergy is buying 25 years of US LNG as a hedge against its own chokepoint. The evidence for a corridor is weaker: Oman-Iran talks, and the World Bank's forecast of a partial recovery from Q1 2027. I therefore move five percentage points of probability from the fast-reopening state to the prolonged state. The shift raises the mean FY2027 outcome without moving the most likely outcome, which remains the gradual reopening.

So what: the environment helps Shell's segments very unevenly. Because about 80% of Shell's LNG volume is priced off Brent with a three-to-six-month lag, the coming gas oversupply hits mainly the uncontracted 20%, trading margins and the price slopes on contract renewals, not the whole LNG book.

Counter-case. The disruption persists through 2027 and beyond. When it ends, OPEC+ cannot or will not flood the market, because spare capacity is thin and non-OPEC supply growth peaks in early 2027, and Brent settles at USD 80-90 rather than 70. Morgan Stanley's post-Q3 deck is this case: Brent falls to USD 75 only by Q4 2027, the refining margin is USD 25 in 2027, and FY2027 EPS is USD 6.86. The case is plausible (25%), and it is the state in which Shell earns USD 39bn in 2027 after about USD 2bn of new levies.
What would change my view. Hormuz transits rising above 20 a day for a month, or a formal settlement, would point to a reopening. Damage to Shell's own Gulf assets (about 20% of Shell's production is in the Middle East) would point the other way. An EU-wide windfall-tax decision would cap the upside state. A fall in the US 10-year yield below 4.5% would signal the rotation of investors out of energy as an inflation hedge.

Market against my view. Consensus has timed the down-leg for 2027 (FY2027 EPS -17%, FY2028 a further -8.5%). Brokers' FY2027 decks span USD 60-100 Brent, and the consensus mean rests on about USD 80-85 with elevated refining margins. I agree with the shape and with the mean. I differ in two ways: the single most likely path (a gradual reopening) sits below the mean, and the headwinds are more pro-cyclical than the market narrative allows.

Conclusion: the operating environment offers an exceptional but transient supply-scarcity tailwind that is at its peak, and its headwinds (taxes, demand destruction, the LNG wave and rates) strengthen the longer the tailwind lasts. The environment's skew for the next 12-24 months is therefore negative for earnings from today's spot prices.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. The external force behind 2026 (Hormuz shut, Brent above USD 100, a USD 42 refining margin against a USD 10 mid-cycle, TTF above EUR 100) is a scarcity windfall at its peak that takes about USD 13bn from earnings as it unwinds over FY2027-28, and its direct threats (windfall levies, demand destruction, the 2028-30 LNG wave, 5-10% service inflation, rates) grow the longer it lasts; the moderate structural supports (LNG demand +6% a year, plateauing oil demand, industry capital discipline) only partly offset, and consensus EPS and sales growth for next year at the 2nd percentile confirm the reversal. I put it below the groups' 46 because over the two-to-three-year horizon the forces clearly subtract from growth and margins, well above Maersk's collapse (8) but like Zegona's weak environment, so between Fevertree (38) and Zegona (33).

2Internally-driven corporate change forces

Under Wael Sawan (CEO since January 2023) and Sinead Gorman (CFO since 2022), Shell has delivered a complete self-help programme early. The programme is now in its harvest phase: it underwrites the cash and per-share lines with unusual confidence but adds little to earnings beyond what consensus already carries.

Inference: internal change gives high confidence in the controllables and little incremental earnings. Capex, costs, distributions and the share count are highly predictable. The only earnings gains still to come are volumes, synergies and the chemicals clean-up, and consensus already holds all three.

The one novel internal step is a policy change, not an operational one. A dividend-growth reset or a new cost target at the February Capital Markets Update is the only internal change not yet in the numbers, and it is a multiple event rather than an earnings event.

Reserve life is slow, well known and beyond the 18-month window, but it caps the multiple. Shell's demonstrated answer to its short reserve life is acquisition paid for with shares, and the market discounts that answer.

So what. Model the controllables at guidance or slightly better: capex at the low end of the range, buybacks above the floor and dividend growth of 6%. Add no earnings for self-help beyond the model's USD 3.5bn. Expect 2027 reported earnings to be about USD 4bn below adjusted earnings.

Counter-case. The February update is bigger than I expect: a 10% dividend policy (Morgan Stanley's call), a cost target above USD 7bn, a credible post-2030 resource plan built on ARC, LNG Canada Phase 2, Bonga North (a USD 5bn final investment decision, 110 kb/d at peak) and Gato do Mato, and a chemicals transaction near USD 8bn. That package would be a genuine new internal change force, and the market would re-rate the company-specific part of the multiple.
What would change my view. A buyback announced on 4-Feb-27 below USD 4bn, which would signal cash being kept for acquisitions; a second ARC-sized deal funded in shares; Attachie's reserves written down in the March 20-F. In the other direction: ARC synergies ahead of the USD 250m targeted by September 2027, and a chemicals deal at the top of the range.

Market against my view. The sell-side credits the delivery record fully and half-expects the dividend reset (consensus dividend growth 5.5%; Redburn 6%; RBC 20%). I agree on delivery and on a 6-8% reset. I give less credit than the bulls to ARC: ARC earns about USD 7/boe against USD 12-20/boe for the legacy portfolio, so a 13% volume addition is only a 3-4% earnings addition. I also give more weight to the fact that nominal costs are no longer falling.

Conclusion: Shell's self-help programme is strong, credible, well executed and now in its harvest phase. It underwrites the cash and per-share lines with unusual confidence but adds little to earnings beyond what consensus carries. Its one novel step, a distribution-policy reset dated for 4-Feb-27, is a multiple event rather than an earnings event.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. A complete self-help programme delivered early (USD 5.83bn of structural cost out by mid-2026, capex at or below guide, refineries 15 to 7, a long list of exits, buybacks of at least USD 3bn for 19 quarters and the count down 27% since 2019) plus a large strategic move into Canada (ARC, lifting the production CAGR from 1% to 4%, and the LNG Canada Phase 2 FID) underwrites about USD 3.5bn of banked self-help and a 5% a year share-count fall within three years. It is held back by the harvest phase (nominal opex no longer falling), ARC paid 75% in dilutive stock at about USD 7/boe, the shortest reserve life among peers, thinning capability and a coming chemicals write-down, so I agree with the groups' 62: an ordinary-to-good positive between OEM (66) and Odfjell Drilling (61).

3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Shell is an above-average business with a concentrated, genuine moat in LNG and trading. The moat widens with volatility, which is why 2026 is so good and why the calmer, oversupplied LNG market of 2027-30 will narrow it.

The industry structure supports returns but is fragile. A cartel with a record of price wars (2014-16 and March 2020) and geopolitics set the crude price. LNG has no cartel and faces a 2028-30 supply wave. Asian and Middle Eastern capacity additions set refining and chemical margins. Politicians tax windfalls.

Three features of the industry protect incumbents. Entry barriers are real: LNG costs above USD 1,000 per tonne of annual capacity, deepwater projects need large capital, and concessions are sovereign. Discipline among the majors has held through two windfalls. Consolidation favours the advantaged players (ExxonMobil-Pioneer, Chevron-Hess, Adura, Saipem-Subsea 7).

Suppliers now have pricing power for the first time in a decade. Three firms take 98% of subsea tree awards, subsea engineering, procurement, construction and installation costs rise 5-10% a year, and no new rigs are being built. Shell's fixed capex budget of USD 20-22bn therefore buys 5-10% less activity each year.

Shell is number one or two where it earns its premium. It has the largest listed LNG portfolio (about 20% of global demand, twice TotalEnergies'), 45 mtpa of operating liquefaction, one of the two largest integrated trading houses, the largest retail network (44,109 sites) and the number one lubricants brand for 19 years.

The 2026 crisis was a live test of the LNG and trading moat, and Shell passed it. In Q2, Integrated Gas beat consensus by 11% while its production fell 31% from the previous quarter. In Q3, Integrated Gas earned USD 3.04bn (+42% year on year) on production 21% lower, through near-record sourcing of third-party cargoes. TotalEnergies' gas trading missed by 10% in the same market.

Shell is mid-table in upstream. Production is 2.7-2.8 mboe/d, rising to about 3.4 with ARC by 2027; the upstream unit cost is USD 8.54/boe against under USD 5 at TotalEnergies; reserve life is the lowest of the European group.

Pricing power in the usual sense is minimal. Shell takes the market price on almost all its revenue. Its "pricing" is a volatility rent earned in market dislocations, plus a small genuine premium in Marketing: premium fuels are 13.5% of volume but 26% of gross mobility margin.

Shell's financial profile is solid rather than outstanding. Return on average capital employed (ROACE) was 12.8-13.4% in 2023, 11.3% in 2024, 9.4% in 2025 and 12.4% annualised in Q2 2026. Mid-cycle ROACE is about 11-12%, against 12.6-13.9% at TotalEnergies and 14.5% at Equinor.

Cash conversion is strong but noisy. At normal prices, about 1.0-1.1x of adjusted earnings turns into lease-adjusted free cash flow, but working capital swings by up to USD 11bn a quarter and cash taxes lag the tax charge.

The balance sheet is strong. Net debt was USD 39.7bn at Q3, including about USD 30bn of leases; gearing is 16.6% (2.7% excluding leases); credit ratings are A+ / AA-. The buyback floor holds at USD 50 Brent, and the dividend breakeven near USD 40 is shared only with TotalEnergies and Eni.

Earnings quality is the weak point of the financial profile. Impairments of USD 8.3bn, 4.4bn and 3.7bn in 2023-25 sit outside adjusted earnings. USD 9.5bn of FY2025 revenue came from Level 3 derivative fair values, which rest on unobservable inputs. About USD 45bn of capital underperforms (Jefferies), much of it in chemicals.

Sawan is an excellent operator and capital allocator, judged on his actions. Everything he said he would do has been done, fast, and benchmarked against buybacks. Shell's communication is among the best in the sector for modellers (frameworks, sensitivities, pre-close update notes and quarterly segment ranges) and opaque exactly where the surprises come from (trading, and tax by jurisdiction).

The management team is competent, cohesive and insular. There have been no external senior hires, and the head of mergers and acquisitions resigned over the BP decision. Ambition is narrow by design: per-share value over volume. The culture is "harsher" and strained by restructuring. Pay is aligned: the CEO's shareholding is 900% of salary, and the long-term incentive plan pays on normalised free cash flow per share and relative total shareholder return.

So what. The financial profile and the management justify modelling the controllables close to guidance and expecting the frameworks to survive a downturn. They do not justify a growth multiple.

Counter-case. Shell's trading-and-LNG franchise is a durable, repeatable earnings engine: a baseline of about USD 7bn of net operating profit a year, worth 2-4 points of ROACE and demonstrated across cycles. That engine deserves a quality premium the market has never paid, because it is opaque. The chemicals exit and the renewables clean-up lift ROACE toward 13%, and ARC and LNG Canada Phase 2 answer the longevity question for a decade. On that reading, Shell is the best capital allocator in Europe trading at a discount.
What would change my view. Disclosure of the trading contribution, which would let the market value the trading baseline; the chemicals exit at a non-distressed price; a reconciliation of reserve life showing 9.5 years after adding ARC's 2bn boe of proved and probable reserves.

Market against my view. The market rates TotalEnergies as the quality name: its sell-side buy share is 58% against Shell's 39%, and it is the only major with a C valuation rating on the dashboard, against Shell's D. I think Shell's quality is real but sits in the volatile layer, which is why the market under-rates it in calm markets and why it over-earns in dislocated ones. I agree with the market that TotalEnergies' organic growth and reserve life make it the more robust foundation.

Conclusion: Shell is an above-average business with a concentrated, genuine moat in LNG and trading, a disciplined and reliable management team and a strong balance sheet. It is held back by a mid-table upstream with the shortest reserve life among European peers, moderate returns and noisy earnings quality. It is a B-grade foundation that supports a yield multiple, not a growth one.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. Qualitatively Shell has one genuine, widening moat (the largest LNG portfolio with physically backed trading, proven in 2026 when Integrated Gas beat by 11% on 31% lower production) and an excellent, aligned management, but it is a price-taker in a cartel- and geopolitics-priced industry with a mid-table upstream (unit cost USD 8.54/boe against under 5 at TotalEnergies), the shortest reserve life in the group and a profit line of low predictability. The financial profile is solid rather than strong (ROIC 7.2%, 54th percentile; mid-cycle ROACE 11-12% with noisy earnings quality and about USD 45bn of underperforming capital, offset by A+/AA- and 2.7% ex-lease gearing), consistent with the groups (52 / 55 / 55 / 70); less predictable than Helios Towers' contracted economics but better than Vodafone's restructuring perimeter.

4Conservative guidance, sell-side management, track record of delivery and upgrades

Shell's guidance is conservative and its record of meeting it is near-perfect. Because Shell guides frameworks rather than earnings, that conservatism protects the distributions, not the EPS estimates.

Shell does not guide earnings; it guides frameworks, and it set those frameworks for a world of USD 60-70 Brent.

Shell changes its frameworks only at Capital Markets Days (June 2023, March 2025, and now 4-Feb-27), and it reports windfalls without upgrading. Dividend growth under Sawan averaged 2.1% a year before 2026 (Morgan Stanley), below inflation; the 5% rise in 2026 broke that pattern.

The 2026 distributions sit at the bottom of the "sacrosanct" range. Even after the USD 5bn buyback quarter, 2026 distributions will land at about 39-40% of cash flow from operations, against 50% before the crisis. That gap is the room for a February raise.

Inference: take guidance as a floor for capital returns and a ceiling for capex. Guidance is conservative in every dimension, and more so once realised prices are taken into account. The conservatism protects the distributions, not the EPS estimates, because the estimates are price-deck calls that the company does not make. The gap that matters is between consensus and the deck.

The probability that Shell raises its frameworks at the February update is better than even. The probability that it cuts any framework is under 5%: only a fast reopening plus an OPEC+ volume push would return the buyback to the USD 3bn floor, and that would be a return to the floor, not a breach of it.

So what. Shell's update notes mean the next two quarterly prints will land within about 5% of the consensus that forms after each note, so expect two more beats of low single digits. The February update is the one dated event at which guidance, estimates and narrative move together in the case's favour.

Counter-case. Management banks the windfall. Gorman has said that building cash gives "flexibility to accelerate buybacks during cycle downturns"; management has never named the gearing level at which it stops retaining cash; and the pattern since 2023 is to raise only targets that have already been met. A 4% dividend and a USD 3.5bn buyback in February, with Brent already falling, would read as cash kept for acquisitions and would hit the company-specific part of the multiple.
What would change my view. The wording on trading in the Q4 update note ("significantly higher" or "lower"); Brent on 4-Feb-27 (above USD 90 supports a bigger reset; below USD 70 argues for caution).

Market against my view. The market expects the frameworks to be met and half-expects the dividend reset: consensus dividend growth is about 5.5%, Morgan Stanley's 10% is the most-cited call, and RBC expects 20%. I sit at 6%, a little above consensus and well below the bulls. I think the market's reaction will depend as much on the buyback and the resource plan as on the dividend number.

Conclusion: Shell's guidance is conservative and its record of meeting and beating guidance is near-perfect. Because Shell guides frameworks rather than earnings, the conservatism protects distributions rather than EPS estimates, and the most likely raise, a dividend reset to 6-8% on 4-Feb-27, is already half in the price.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. Shell guides frameworks rather than earnings and the record on them is near-perfect for three years (capex below guide each year, costs two and a half years early, 2025 distributions above range, projects at 99.8% of budget) with conservative frameworks set for a USD 60-70 world and better-than-even odds of a raise on 4-Feb-27. It is held below the high 70s because against estimates it beats only in volatile markets and missed by about 10% in Q4 2025 and Q2 2023, raises only at CMDs, and does nothing to keep EPS consensus conservative (the groups' 42 on estimates beside 68 on guidance), so between Maersk (75) and Linea Directa (69).

5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out scope and feedback loops

Shell's leverage is price leverage on a fixed cost base: it doubled EPS in 2026 and works in reverse from here. The feedback loops that reward shareholders run through cash and the share count, not through profit, and they work best for a buyer at a lower share price.

Operating leverage is high to price. Operating costs of about USD 35.7bn and depreciation and amortisation of about USD 24bn are fixed against both volume and price, so changes in realised prices fall almost straight through to pre-tax profit.

Volume leverage is weak, because the new barrels earn low margins. ARC's barrels earn about USD 7/boe, so a 15-20% rise in production lifts mid-cycle earnings by only about 11%.

Financial leverage is almost irrelevant to EPS. Net interest of USD 3.1-3.8bn is 7-9% of pre-tax profit, and each USD 10bn of net debt is worth only about USD 0.06 a share. A 1% rise in interest rates improves pre-tax income by USD 148m, because Shell's cash exceeds its floating-rate debt.

The scope for further cost-out is spent. Gross savings of up to USD 7bn by 2028 are matched by inflation and carbon costs. The remaining cost gain comes from exits, chiefly chemicals, worth about USD 0.3-0.5bn.

Six feedback loops act on Shell, and they split cleanly. The three balancing loops act on the profit line and hurt a holder. The three counter-cyclical or reinforcing loops act on the cash and per-share lines and help a holder. Because the buyback retires more shares at a lower price, EPS outcomes are less dispersed than net-income outcomes.

Inference and so what. Shell's model did turn revenue growth into outsized profit growth in 2026, and the same gearing now works in reverse. The per-share engine is about half as powerful per dollar as it was in 2022-24, because buybacks then were made at 5-9x forward earnings against about 11x today.

Counter-case. The windfall lasts long enough (the prolonged state) for the balance-sheet loop to do real work. USD 10-15bn of unused balance-sheet capacity by 2028, spent on buybacks, adds 1.5-2% a year to per-share accretion, and the Marketing premium and the trading baseline hold mid-cycle EBITDA at USD 65-67bn rather than USD 60bn.
What would change my view. Disclosure of trading profit that showed the trading baseline growing with LNG volumes; a sustained recovery in the AECO price (the Alberta gas price hub) above CAD 3, which would lift ARC's margin per barrel.

Market against my view. Consensus understands the price leverage, which is in every model, and under-models the per-share loop: consensus implies about 3.5% a year of share-count reduction against the model's 5%. I agree with the market on the shape of profit and differ on the share count, which is worth about 3% of FY2029 EPS.

Conclusion: Shell's leverage is price leverage on a fixed cost base, which doubled EPS in 2026 and will cut it by about 20% in 2027 and about 30% by 2028. The reinforcing loops that reward shareholders (working-capital release, buybacks at a lower price, and debt repaid in the windfall) run through cash and the share count rather than profit, and they work best for a buyer at a lower share price.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. The structure has real leverage to price, not to volume: about USD 60bn of opex and D&A are fixed, so FY2026 revenue +39% became EPS +102% and FY2027 revenue -17% becomes EPS -20%, but Shell takes rather than sets price, the new barrels are low-margin (ARC about USD 7/boe, so 15-20% more volume lifts mid-cycle earnings about 11%), cost-out scope is spent against inflation and carbon, and financial leverage is negligible (net interest 7-9% of pre-tax). The only reinforcing loop that works for holders runs through cash and the share count (buybacks retiring about 5% a year, working-capital release), so this is the ordinary mix with price gearing proven only in a scarcity cycle, slightly above 50 and coherent with Economic strength at 55.

Three features define the forecast.

First, volumes rise while earnings fall. Volumes rise 15-20% in 2027 while earnings fall 21%. The new barrels are worth about USD 2.0bn in 2027 against about USD 9bn lost to the lower price deck. The Qatar volumes return only when the Strait reopens, and the reopening is also what lowers the price, so Shell is long the disruption by four to five times its volume exposure.

Second, Chemicals & Products carries the fall while Integrated Gas rises. Integrated Gas earnings rise in FY2027 because of the LNG price lag, a full year of ARC and a 70% average restoration of the Qatar volumes. Chemicals & Products carries 60% of the group's decline, because Products trading earned 126% of the segment's 2025 profit and the refining margin normalises from USD 42.

Third, the mid-cycle is structurally better than 2025. Mid-cycle adjusted EBITDA of USD 65-67bn equals 2024's level at a Brent price about USD 8 lower. FY2028-30 EPS of USD 4.65-4.86 is 45-55% above 2025: about 45% of that gain is Shell's own structure, 30% the lower share count and 25% a slightly better price deck.

Double-digit growth exists only when measured from the 2025 base. From today there is no growth at the headline level: EPS falls about 30% from FY2026 to FY2028 and then grows 4-5% a year, entirely through the buyback, while net income drifts down about 1% a year at a flat price deck. Measured from the 2025 base, which management uses for its target of "free cash flow per share growth above 10% a year to 2030", the growth is real and double-digit. Margins are structurally higher than in 2023-25, by about USD 6-8bn of EBITDA at a given deck, but they will not be higher than in 2026.

The cone for FY2027 adjusted EPS has three states, and free cash flow covers the distributions in all three.

So what. Weight the forecasts the way the record supports: 85-90% confidence in the controllables, about 70% in FY2026 (three quarters are banked), about 40% in FY2027 and 30% beyond. Lean above consensus for FY2026, neutral for FY2027 with the downside heavier in the most likely state, and slightly below consensus for FY2028, because the model uses USD 72 Brent against consensus' 75.

Counter-case. The base case may be too gradual on refining: Morgan Stanley's USD 25 margin for 2027 would add about USD 0.50 to FY2027 EPS. It may be too quick to fade trading. Or it may be too generous on the Qatar restoration: a 70% average in 2027 is high if a settlement arrives only mid-year, and Suez transits were still 50% below their baseline three years after the Red Sea attacks.
What would change my view (and the inputs). Transit data and the export date for Pearl Train 2; the Q4 note's wording on trading; the February buyback; the price and date of the chemicals sale; the AECO gas price. I keep the model's inputs unchanged. The corrections from the third and fourth analysis sets (the revenue base, cash timing, USD 16bn of 2027 buybacks, 6% dividend growth and the North West Shelf proceeds) are the right ones, and the Q3 print validated the segment build to the decimal.

Market against my view. The model is 3.6% above consensus for FY2026 (because Q4 is priced off USD 105 Brent), level for FY2027 and 3% below for FY2028. The broker range for FY2027 EPS (USD 3.95 to 7.71) is the cone of Hormuz states, not a disagreement about Shell; consensus is the cone's average, and almost no single path ends near it. Consensus revenue is stale (it implies product prices that do not match consensus' own EBITDA), so the model's revenue gap of -8.6% in FY2027 is not an earnings view.

Conclusion: the forecasts describe a two-year normalisation from a USD 37bn windfall to a USD 23-24bn mid-cycle that is USD 5-6bn better than 2025. EPS falls about 30% from FY2026 to FY2028 and then grows 4-5% a year through the buyback alone. Double-digit growth exists only measured from the 2025 base, the FY2027 figure sits in a cone three times the normal width, and the cash and distribution lines are the forecasts to trust.

Score: 21, set by the Rater. Earnings fall about 30% from the FY2026 windfall to FY2028 and then grow 4-5% a year through the buyback alone while net income drifts down about 1% a year, so the measure gives F and there is no organic route to double-digit growth. I place it at the top of the band because the fall is a one-off peak rolling off to a mid-cycle 45-55% above FY2025 (about +10% a year from the 2025 base) with EBITDA margins structurally above 2023-25 at a given deck, coherent with the groups' 27.

7Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and narrative over 6-12 months

Estimates are likely to rise for the next two prints and the February update, then be cut from mid-2027 in the two most likely states. The 6-12 month upgrade path is a rise and a fall that nets to roughly nothing, and the narrative already carries almost all the good news.

The near-term upgrade has a clear source: the pre-Q3 consensus under-estimated Q4 2026. The pre-Q3 FY2026 consensus of USD 36.1bn implied only about USD 8.5bn for Q4. The model's Q4 is USD 9.95bn, and Morgan Stanley's full year is USD 38bn. Q4 Brent is near USD 105 and TTF above EUR 100; the oil-indexed LNG lag carries Q3-Q4 prices into Q1 2027; and the USD 5bn buyback lowers every broker's share count.

Estimates are already moving toward spot prices. Consensus FY2027 EPS has risen 21% in three months and 15% in one month. Redburn raised its 2026-28 estimates by 5% after Q3 (FY2027 USD 5.30), and Morgan Stanley moved to USD 6.86 with a USD 25 refining margin. Revision breadth is positive (FY2027 EBITDA +6% / +13% / +17% over one, three and six months; target price +2% / +7% / +5%).

The update notes are compressing the size of Shell's beats. After beats of 8-10% in H1, the Q3 beat was 5%. The narrative ("set up for a long cycle", Jefferies; the dividend reset as the re-rating catalyst, Morgan Stanley) is coherent and widely held.

The expected path of estimates has three phases.

  1. November 2026 to 4-Feb-27: upgrades. FY2026 rises to about USD 37.5-38bn. FY2027 rises 5-10%, toward USD 5.6-5.9, as Q1 2027 is marked to the forward curve and the LNG lag. The Q4 print beats the post-note consensus by low single digits.
  2. February to May 2027: per-share revisions. The Capital Markets Update converts cash into per-share revisions (dividend per share up, share count down) without changing net income. Q1 2027 results (early May) still carry Q4 2026 oil prices through the lag and Brent near USD 88 in the base case, so they meet or beat. The first visible trading normalisation appears in the Q1 update note.
  3. June to December 2027: cuts, in the two most likely states. Brent falls to USD 74-72 in the second half, the indicative refining margin falls toward USD 12-15, chemicals run near breakeven, trading returns to its baseline, and Shell's own misses cluster in calm quarters. FY2027 consensus returns to about USD 5.0-5.3, and FY2028 is trimmed toward the model's 4.68 as the long-run deck settles nearer USD 70 than 75. Net revision breadth turns negative. The sell-side buy share (39%, up nine points in six months) is more likely to fall than rise.

The two other states change the timing, not the shape. In the fast-reopening state, the up-leg is cut short in January, and FY2027 consensus falls to USD 4.2-4.5 by mid-year with broad cuts, because almost every broker's 2027 deck is above USD 70. In the prolonged state, FY2027 rises toward USD 6.5-7.0, but the market starts to price the eventual reopening and the taxes, so the shares respond less than the estimates.

The narrative misses little that favours the case.

Inference and so what. The end-points of the upgrade path, probability-weighted (about USD 4.3 at 30%, 5.1 at 45% and 6.8 at 25%), give about USD 5.3, where consensus already stands. Momentum is most favourable, and the valuation most exposed, at the February event. The precedent is strong: after the 2008, 2011-14 and 2022 peaks, consensus was cut for several quarters because price decks lagged the oil price (BP's estimates for seven straight quarters; ExxonMobil's 2024 earnings came in 40% below 2022).

Counter-case. The disruption persists and the sell-side spends 2027 chasing spot prices upward, as Morgan Stanley already has. FY2027 EPS ends near USD 7 and FY2028 near 5.8, and Shell beats every quarter on trading. This is the 25% state, and it is the only state in which upgrade momentum lasts the full year.
What would change my view. Hormuz transits; the Q4 update note; whether February's buyback is USD 4bn or more; the first wording on Q1 2027 trading.

Market against my view. The first analysis set judged that the setup of easy beats was fading; I think there are two more beats and then a reversal. The market's blended FY2027 number is a fair estimate of the mean and a poor estimate of any single path. The dispersion of outcomes is the point.

Conclusion: upgrades to FY2026-27 estimates are likely for the next two prints and the February update, after which consensus is cut from mid-2027 in the two most likely states. The 6-12 month upgrade path is therefore a rise and a fall that nets to roughly nothing, and the narrative already carries almost all the good news.

Guidance, which counts most, is more likely raised than cut at the 4-Feb-27 update (dividend growth above 4% about 55%, a USD 4-5bn buyback about 65%, cut under 5%), but it raises distributions rather than an earnings line; consensus EPS rises 5-10% into February and then, in the 6-12 month window from May to November 2027, is cut back to today's level or lower in 70% of states (probability-weighted end-point about USD 5.3 against consensus 5.28), and the narrative already holds the good news with the buy share more likely to fall. Upgrades already taken (+21% in three months) are momentum, not scope; I sit below the groups' 55 because the window falls on the cut leg, between RELX (50) and Tele2 (44).

8Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price, and the peers

Momentum is strong and broad on every measure, but it is late-stage and crowded. It argues for holding through February, not for buying.

The estimate upgrades sit in the windfall years. Over one, three, six and twelve months, FY2027 EPS revisions are +11% / +21% / +18% / +39% and FY2026 revisions +12% / +24% / +29% / +93%, while FY2028 revisions are only +2% / +4% / -2% / +3%.

The peers share the momentum and the high valuation. Every major in the dashboard's sector carries a B technical rating. Earnings momentum is rated A at Equinor, TotalEnergies, Repsol, Galp, Aker BP and Var Energi, and B at Shell, BP and Eni. Valuation is rated D or F everywhere except TotalEnergies (C). Shell sits at the 70th percentile of its own ten-year P/E range against a peer median above the 80th: it is neither the most nor the least re-rated.

Peers' post-Q3 capital returns differ. Eni raised its buyback and paid a special dividend; TotalEnergies reaffirmed its framework; BP has reached its net-debt target and will restart buybacks late in 2027; Equinor held its buyback flat and is the pure geopolitical hedge (+86% in 2026).

Positioning is crowded. Energy positioning is at the 69th percentile and systematic commodity allocations at the 91st. The Fitness for Fighting momentum tilt turned Underweight on 23-Oct-26. Morgan Stanley's view of 5-Nov-26 is that much of the sector's 42% rally is in the price ("longer disruption priced out").

Inference: the momentum is late in its cycle. The revisions are concentrated in the windfall years, and the price is at its highs together with the whole sector. Company-specific variance has fallen from 57% of Shell's daily moves a year ago to 29%, as the sector trades as one hedge, and the systematic holders who own the hedge are crowded. Shell's company-specific momentum has been positive for six months and is likely to stay mildly positive into February, but it is worth a few points of relative return, not a defence against a sector de-rating.

So what. The momentum reading argues for holding through February and treating the update as the point of maximum favourable information. Resource shares have historically de-rated three to six months before the peak in estimate revisions. If the revision peak comes in mid-2027, the de-rating window opens around the February event.

Counter-case. The sector's leadership is structural rather than cyclical. An inflation regime, an equity bear market in which the cleanest large-cap yield wins, and a decade of under-investment keep energy bid and keep Shell's multiple at the top of its range for years, as in 2017-18, when the two-year-forward P/E held at 12-14x for over a year.
What would change my view. A break below the 50-day average (3,596p) on a de-escalation headline; a fall in the US 10-year yield below 4.5%; a turn in the one-month FY2027 revision to negative.

Market against my view. The market and I read the same data; the difference is the horizon. I read the pinned B / B / D ratings as late-stage, not early-stage.

Conclusion: momentum is strong and broad across estimates, guidance, price and the peer group, but it is late-stage and crowded. The revisions sit in the windfall years, the stock is at its highs with a sector that trades as one hedge, and the momentum is as reversible as the oil price that drives it.

Score: 91, set by the Rater. Both measures are in the top fifth and no part is negative: the buyback stepped up to USD 5bn with a CMU dated, FY2027 EPS revisions +11 / +21 / +18% over one, three and six months (96th percentile at three months; revenue is falling so the growth-scaled ratio is not meaningful, but the size is top-decile), the price at its 52-week high 24% above a rising 200-day average, and peers strong across the sector. I place it low in A because the buy share is only 38% (32nd percentile), FY2028 revisions are flat and positioning is crowded, which the memo reads as late-stage but which does not yet make any part negative.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

The case is simple, binary and unusually trackable, but it is not low-risk. The earnings error and the multiple error are correlated, and the plausible share-price downside in the most likely 18-month path is 25-35%.

The case is simple: one variable, observable weekly. The Hormuz state drives about 85% of the forecast change in earnings, and it is observable every week (Morgan Stanley's transit tracker; Kpler). Once the state is known, the two largest price lines are visible on forward curves. Shell's own disclosure (update notes, segment ranges, published sensitivities and a dated Capital Markets Update) covers the operational building blocks well. By mid-2027 roughly 70% of the FY2027 outcome will be known. Trackability is unusually good for an unusually wide cone.

The dominant share-price risk is sudden and large. A ceasefire or a US-Iran deal would cut oil prices and bond yields together, and energy, the hedge of the current regime, would fund the rotation into other sectors. The 1990 Gulf War analogue took equities down 20% in three months; Equinor's share price fell 30% within months of past normalisations; and the sector memos of October 2026 all find a record margin being capitalised as a run rate.

Shell's trough arithmetic gives falls of a quarter to two-fifths, and more than half in the extreme. The cushions are real: a dividend yield of about 3-4% at trough prices, a buyback of 6-8% of the market value, ex-lease net debt near zero, and a beta of 0.83, which means Shell falls less than its higher-beta peers.

Precedent says forecasts made at price peaks overshoot. The sector underperforms when a peak margin is capitalised, when capex surges, when the oil price collapses or when windfall taxes arrive; Shell fits the first and the fourth today. Forecasts made at the price peaks of 2008, 2011-14 and 2022 overshot because price decks adjusted with a lag.

Shell's distribution framework is built to flex rather than break. Shell's 2020 dividend cut (dividend per share from USD 1.87 to 0.63) is the reason the current framework flexes. The framework has not yet been tested by a real price collapse under this management, but 2025, at USD 69 Brent and a 9.4% ROACE, delivered every commitment.

So what. The risk is not that Shell fails; the risk is that the share price was set in a regime that ends. Position sizing should reflect a plausible drawdown of 25-35% in the most likely 18-month path, cushioned by a cash yield of 9-10% at the trough.

Counter-case. Simplicity cuts both ways. If the Strait stays shut, every fragility above except taxes works in the holder's favour, and the cash lines are robust enough for the distributions to survive every state. A holder who is paid 8% a year in cash to wait for the Strait's state to resolve is not taking the risk a growth-stock holder takes.
What would change my view. Disclosure of trading profit, which would narrow the quarterly noise; an EU-wide windfall-tax decision, which would cap the upside state; Hormuz transits.

Market against my view. Options imply only a 1.5% risk-neutral probability of the shares falling below 1,697p within 12 months (Morgan Stanley), and the sell-side's lowest target is 25% below the price. I think the market under-prices the correlation between the earnings error and the multiple error, and over-prices the durability of the hedge regime.

Conclusion: the case is simple, binary and unusually trackable, but it is not low-risk. The earnings error and the multiple error are correlated, the plausible share-price downside in the most likely 18-month path is 25-35%, and the case's simplicity makes the risk easy to see rather than small.

Score: 33, set by the Rater. The memo's FY2027 EPS cone of USD 4.2 / 5.3 / 7.0 (about -21% to +32%, three times normal width) rests on one exogenous variable whose resolution is sudden (a ceasefire), and the multiple error is correlated with the earnings error, so the most likely 18-month path carries a 25-35% drawdown; quarterly trading surprises of about 10% and a USD 2-4bn gap between reported and adjusted earnings add noise. It is lifted above the 25 level by unusual trackability (weekly transits), mechanical cash lines (buyback floor to USD 50 Brent, ex-lease net debt near zero) and stable management, so it sits just above BP's commodity-and-governance risk and below D'Ieteren, coherent with the groups' 38 and 33.

10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Shell is in the late reinforcing phase of a windfall-driven cycle. The 4-Feb-27 update is the probable peak of the narrative, and a transition to stalling by mid-2027 is the most likely outcome.

Evidence: the markers of the reinforcing phase are all present. The dashboard's rule places Shell in the Reinforcing phase, and the markers fit: three consecutive beats, a buyback step-up, estimates rising for two years, a dated catalyst with a coherent bull narrative (the dividend reset), the price at its highs on a rising 200-day average, and eight points of company-specific outperformance over six months. The first and third analysis sets agree that Shell is in the reinforcing phase of its narrative and in the late, already-rewarded phase of the sector's outperformance template: payout frameworks are believed, companies guide low and beat, the transition discount has been removed, and the starting multiple in 2022-23 was a depressed 5-7x.

Inference: the phase is late, and the transition is dated and visible. In the base case the Strait reopens gradually through H1 2027. Earnings then fall about 35% year on year by Q2 2027, revisions turn negative, trading becomes a source of misses, and the narrative shifts from "long cycle" to "normalisation", which marks the stalling phase. In the fast-reopening state the transition comes in Q1 2027 and is sharper. Only in the prolonged state (25%) does the reinforcing phase extend through 2027, and even there the market begins to price the eventual reopening and the taxes. The February update is the last scheduled event at which guidance, estimates and story all move the same way.

So what. For a holder, the lifecycle reading says about three months remain before the phase changes in the two most likely states. For a buyer, the interesting phase is the one after stalling: the new turning-up phase after the sector has de-rated, when the buyback retires 6% of the shares a year at a lower price and the per-share engine works for the buyer.

Counter-case. A dividend reset at 10% and a credible post-2030 plan broaden the thesis from "windfall plus yield" to "yield compounder with longevity", and the stock moves from reinforcing to thesis-broadening rather than stalling. Morgan Stanley's Overweight rating assumes this path.
What would change my view. A 10% dividend policy with a stated buyback pace in February; or Hormuz transits.

Market against my view. The market prices the reinforcing phase, with the multiple at the top of its range. I think the market prices the current phase correctly and the next phase not at all.

Conclusion: Shell is in the late reinforcing phase of a windfall-driven cycle, with the 4-Feb-27 update the probable peak of the narrative and a transition to stalling the most likely state by mid-2027.

Score: 41, set by the Rater. The computed and memo phase of Reinforcing is right for today (three beats, a buyback step-up, price at highs on a rising 200-day average) but it is late and windfall-driven: in the two most likely states (75%) earnings fall about 35% year on year by Q2 2027, revisions turn negative and the narrative moves to normalisation, so stalling is dated about three months out with only the prolonged state extending it. Strong current momentum keeps it a little above National Grid's stalling, but the good news is largely known and a one-off is being priced, so below Linea Directa.

11The fair multiple

The guideline multiple of 11.58x is a peak-phase multiple applied to falling forward earnings. My fair multiple at the 18-month horizon is about 10x, and 11.58x is reachable only if the disruption persists or the February dividend reset is at the 10% end.

The guideline sits at the 90th percentile of Shell's ten-year history. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for the Reinforcing phase is 11.58x two-year-forward earnings, the dashboard's "mania" band. The model's current multiple is 10.9x (25-Oct-26); the dashboard read 10.0x on 6-Nov-26, after the post-Q3 upgrades to forward EPS.

The multiple has exceeded 11.6x in only two episodes in ten years, and never held that level while forward earnings were falling. The first episode, mid-2017 to early 2018 (12-14x), came when forward earnings were depressed and recovering: a turning-up phase on a low base. The second was March 2026 (11.3x), at the outbreak of the conflict.

About three-quarters of Shell's multiple is the sector's regime. The European majors trade together (Shell's six-month correlation is 0.86 with BP, 0.85 with TotalEnergies and 0.81 with Eni), all sit at elevated percentiles of their own history, and all but TotalEnergies carry D or F valuation ratings.

The company-specific quarter of the multiple can be identified. It consists of a defensiveness premium, a discount for trading opacity (Bernstein: 20-25% of the European majors' earnings are valued on low multiples), a discount for reserve life, and an option on the dividend reset. The first analysis set's own anchor for a harvest-and-return model is a yield multiple of about 7-10x P/E, with Redburn's floor of 6.0x enterprise value to debt-adjusted cash flow.

My view: set the fair multiple for the phase Shell will be in at the 18-month horizon. The guideline applies a peak-delivery multiple to a stock whose forward earnings fall about 30% over the horizon and whose phase most likely turns to stalling before the horizon ends. The return is realised at the horizon, so the multiple should be the one that fits the stock at the horizon, not today.

At end-2027, in 70% of states, Shell is a yield stock in a de-rated sector. It will have mid-cycle forward earnings of about USD 4.7, a dividend of USD 1.76 and a buyback of about USD 14bn. The band from the ten-year median to the 75th percentile (9.0-10.3x) is the right range for that stock.

I put the central fair multiple at 10.0x. It sits above the median because Shell's balance sheet, buyback and dividend reset are better than its ten-year average. It sits below the 75th percentile because forward earnings are falling and the reserve-life discount is unanswered. At 10x on EPS of USD 4.66 the shares would be worth USD 46.6, a dividend yield of 3.8% and a total cash yield of about 10%, which is where a defensive yield name with these characteristics has traded.

The 11.58x guideline is reachable in two cases, together perhaps 35% of outcomes. In the first, the disruption persists and the multiple stays a sector hedge for another 14 months while EPS stays elevated. In the second, the February reset is at the 10% end and the market re-rates Shell as a yield compounder.

Counter-case. The ten-year distribution is itself the wrong anchor. It is dominated by the 2019-22 transition discount (5-8x), which the strategy pivot and peers following it have removed, and by the 2020 collapse. On a post-pivot distribution the median is nearer 9.5-10x and the 90th percentile is a normal good year, not mania. US majors trade at 14x 2027 earnings against 9.3x for the Europeans, and the gap is closing as Shell's returns and payout converge on theirs.
What would change my view. Toward 11x: a 10% dividend policy and a stated buyback pace in February, or disclosure of trading profit. Toward 8-9x: a reopening with an OPEC+ volume push. Toward 9x: the US 10-year yield below 4.5%, through the rotation out of energy.

Market against my view. The market pays 10-11x today, close to the guideline, which means it is pricing the current phase and the hedge regime. I think the market is right about the phase today and will not hold the multiple through the transition.

Conclusion: the guideline 11.58x is a peak-phase multiple applied to a stock whose forward earnings are falling and whose multiple is three-quarters a sector regime. My fair multiple at the 18-month horizon is therefore about 10x (within the band from the ten-year median to the 75th percentile), with 11.58x reachable only if the disruption persists or the February dividend reset is at the 10% end.

Score: 51, set by the Rater. Neutral on both measures gives C, and today's 10.0x after the post-Q3 upgrades is close to the memo's own 10x fair multiple, so the dearness is not enough to move the letter. I place it at the floor of the band because the 70th percentile leans dear (the 99th percentile of five years), the peer reading flatters with the whole cohort above the 80th percentile of its own history, and the multiple is applied to windfall-inflated forward earnings that fall about 30%, which a late-reinforcing-to-stalling stock does not deserve to hold.

12Total shareholder return

At the guideline multiple the shares return about 4% over 18 months, almost all of it dividends. At my 10x fair multiple they lose about 10%, so the return case rests on the multiple holding, not on Shell.

At the guideline multiple (the model's calculation). The model starts from a price of GBP 40.33 and a multiple of 10.9x today, and reaches the guideline 11.58x at the 18-month horizon.

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedFrom dividendsFrom the multipleFrom earnings
18 months, to 31-Dec-27+4.3%+3.7%+4.5%+6.7%-6.5%
Three years, to 30-Jun-29+14.0%+5.1%+7.8%+6.7%-0.5%

Dividends do all the work over 18 months. A re-rating of 6.7% (from 10.9x to 11.58x) merely offsets a 6.5% fall in two-year-forward EPS, from about USD 4.98 (a blend of FY2027-28) to about 4.66 (a blend of FY2028-29). The price is therefore flat, and the 4.5% dividend yield is the return.

Over three years, forward EPS stops falling. The FY2029-30 blend of about USD 4.95 is level with today's, because net income drifts down about 1% a year while the share count falls about 5% a year. The same re-rating is still in the number, and dividends of 7.8% give the 14% total.

The buyback sits inside the earnings part of the return. The buyback is why forward EPS falls only 6.5% while forward net income falls about 12%. The third analysis set's cross-check (about +5-7% over 18 months and +15% over three years) is slightly above the model's figures because it carried slightly more cash; the difference changes nothing.

At my fair multiple, and across the states. The arithmetic below applies the model's earnings and dividends, and varies the multiple and, for the two off-base states, the forward EPS.

CaseMultiple at horizonTwo-year-forward EPS at end-202718-month total returnThree-year total return
Guideline (model)11.58x4.66+4.3%+14.0%
My central view10.0x4.66about -10% (multiple -8.3%, earnings -6.5%, dividends +4.5%)about -1% (multiple -8.3%, earnings -0.5%, dividends +7.8%)
Ten-year median9.0x4.66about -18%about -10%
Fast reopening, sector de-rates9.0xabout 4.1about -28%about -22%
Prolonged disruption, regime holds11.58xabout 5.5about +22%about +25%
Probability-weighted (30 / 45 / 25) on my multiples9.0 / 10.0 / 11.58x4.1 / 4.66 / 5.5about -7%about -1%

Inference and so what. The return case rests on the multiple holding at a peak-phase level while earnings fall, not on anything Shell does. A holder at 4,033p is paid about 4.5% a year to carry a position whose plausible 18-month range is -28% to +22% and whose probability-weighted outcome is modestly negative. The components of the return that Shell controls (dividends, and the buyback inside the earnings line) are positive and reliable; the component it does not control (the multiple) is large and skewed down.

The constructive implication: the same arithmetic produces an attractive return from a lower starting price.

Counter-case. If the prolonged state arrives and February brings a 10% dividend policy, the shares deliver about 20% over 18 months with a yield attached, and the sector hedge keeps working. Morgan Stanley's target of 3,961p (-2%) and Jefferies' USD 59.5 (+10%) bracket the sell-side's version of this case.
What would change my view. Any of the multiple triggers in topic 11; and the February buyback, which sets the share count for the earnings line.

Market against my view. The shares trade at the consensus target price (a mean of USD 53.03 against a price of USD 53.98), which says the market expects the dividend and little else over 12 months. I agree with that mean and differ on the dispersion of outcomes and its downward skew.

Conclusion: at the guideline multiple the shares return about 4% over 18 months and 14% over three years, almost all of it dividends, because a 6-7% re-rating merely offsets a 6-7% fall in forward earnings. At my 10x fair multiple the 18-month return is about -10% and the three-year return about nil, so the return case rests on the multiple holding, not on Shell.

Score: 18, set by the Rater. The probability-weighted return on the memo's state multiples is a loss of about 7% (dividends +4.5% against a 6.5% fall in forward EPS and a de-rating to about 10x), with the three-year check near nil, so F, which maps to about 18. I hold it there rather than lower because the cash return is reliable and the prolonged state gives +22%, but the fast-reopening tail of -28% is fat and correlated, so no lift either.

13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Shell is a well-run, financially robust harvest-and-return business with one genuine and widening moat, sitting on a geopolitical windfall that the market has correctly refused to capitalise beyond 2027.

Shell's cash and per-share lines are among the most predictable of any company its size: the buyback floor, the dividend, the capex band and ex-lease net debt near zero survive every state of the world in the analysis. Its profit line is a reading of the Strait of Hormuz, and so is its multiple.

For the next three months, guidance, estimates and narrative move the case's way, culminating in the Capital Markets Update on 4-Feb-27, which will probably reset dividend growth to 6-8% and confirm a USD 4-5bn quarterly buyback. After that, in the two most likely states, earnings normalise by 30-35%, consensus is cut, trading turns from beats to misses, and the sector de-rates together with the earnings.

The guideline multiple of 11.58x prices the current phase, and the current phase is late. At that multiple the shares pay their dividend and little else. At the multiple I think a stalling yield stock will carry, about 10x, the shares lose about 10% over 18 months and make nothing over three years.

The case's practical virtue is that it is simple, binary and trackable from one weekly series, so it can be timed. The per-share engine that makes Shell attractive (buybacks at a lower price, with USD 10-15bn of unused balance-sheet capacity) works hardest for a buyer after the de-rating, not before it.

34Thesis's Change Forces' Strength

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 34, set by the Rater. The external force (35) is the dominant one, driving about 85% of the forecast earnings change and reversing from a peak, while the credible internal programme (63) gives back only about USD 3bn, half of it waiting on the same Strait; together they turn into falling forecast profits (topic 6 F, EPS down about 30% to FY2028), so the net change is clearly negative, lifted off the 25 level only because the mid-cycle lands above the 2025 past and the per-share engine surely reaches EPS.

65Foundations' Robustness

Foundations' Robustness: 65, set by the Rater. A genuine LNG-and-trading moat, an A+/AA- balance sheet with 2.7% ex-lease gearing, a buyback floor at USD 50 Brent and a dividend breakeven near USD 40, and a management that has delivered every controllable (topic 4 at 70) make the business robust in every state, above Judges Scientific's 60; it stays below the 75 band because quality (topic 3 at 58) rests on a price-taking commodity structure with a mid-table upstream, the shortest reserve life among peers and an unpredictable profit line.

20Setups' Fit/Crispness

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 20, set by the Rater. The best-fitting setup is a Mechanical EPS Upgrader and the per-share engine is real and evidenced (buybacks at least USD 3bn for 19 quarters, count down 27%), but the case lacks the element the setup needs most, a durable EPS step-up: forecast EPS falls about 30% as a supply-shock windfall rolls off, so in substance it is close to the inverse of the setup, a windfall at the point the setup would sell, and I agree with the memo's D at the weak end.

31Case Riskiness

Case Riskiness: 31, set by the Rater. The case is simple and trackable from one weekly series and carries no balance-sheet or franchise risk, but it is a single exogenous binary driver with an EPS cone of about -21% to +32% whose error is correlated with a sector-driven multiple, so the most likely path holds a 25-35% drawdown (topic 9 at 33); that places it near the 25 level for a single-driver case with a wide range, lifted slightly by the cash cushion and the trackability.

Consensus is the FactSet median of 25-Oct-26 unless a later note is named, and consensus estimates are shown by named financial year (FY2026, FY2027, FY2028), never on a rolling basis.

  3. Analysis sets. References to the first, second, third and fourth analysis sets are to the earlier rounds of analysis behind this memo; the second set supplies the post-tax price sensitivities, and the third and fourth sets supply the model corrections kept in topic 6.
  4. Hormuz states. The three states are a fast reopening by Q1 2027 (30%), a gradual reopening through H1 2027 (45%, the base case) and disruption through 2027 (25%).
  5. Total-return basis. The total-return split is on the two-year-forward basis: the multiple and the two-year-forward EPS today against each horizon. The multiple and earnings parts multiply; dividends add. The horizons are the model's fixed columns.
  6. Sources of visuals. Default visuals are from the Financial Analyst's model after update 2, FactSet and the Master Dashboard; the five financial tables are FactSet's, checked cell by cell.   7. Scores. Topic scores and the four overall grades are set by the Rater; the comparison names in each score reason (for example Maersk, Zegona or Linea Directa) are the Rater's reference companies, and "the groups" are the Rater's peer groups.
  8. Abbreviations and units. LNG: liquefied natural gas. TTF: Title Transfer Facility, the Dutch benchmark gas price. AECO: the Alberta gas price hub. ARC: ARC Resources. CMU / CMD: Capital Markets Update / Capital Markets Day. FID: final investment decision. CFFO: cash flow from operations. ROACE: return on average capital employed. ROIC: return on invested capital. CAGR: compound annual growth rate. LTIP: long-term incentive plan. PMI: purchasing managers' index. SEC: US Securities and Exchange Commission. 2P: proved plus probable reserves. Level 3: fair values based on unobservable inputs. bbl: barrel. boe: barrel of oil equivalent. mb: million barrels. mb/d, mboe/d and kb/d, kboe/d: million and thousand barrels (of oil equivalent) a day. mtpa: million tonnes a year. mmbtu: million British thermal units.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
